content:
This is a radiology (MRI) report. In plain language, it says:

- The uterus looks normal in size, shape and internal structure.
- There is a round/oval mass in front of and to the left of the uterus measuring about 5.2 x 7.6 cm.
- The mass contains fat (it shows fat signal on MRI) and also has a small area of tissue that does not take up contrast.
- These MRI features are most typical of a teratoma (often called a dermoid cyst), which is a common type of ovarian tumor that usually contains fat, sometimes bone, teeth or other tissue.
- The ovaries could not be clearly seen on the scan (the mass may be arising from one of the ovaries and obscuring it).
- There are no signs of spread: the bladder, pelvic organs, bones, muscles and lymph nodes looked normal and there were no fluid collections.

What this likely means for you
- The lesion is probably a benign ovarian teratoma (mature cystic teratoma/dermoid). These are common and usually noncancerous.
- Your clinician asked for tumor markers—these are blood tests (for example CA-125, AFP, beta-hCG, sometimes LDH) used to help evaluate ovarian masses and to look for features that might suggest malignancy.
- Because the ovaries weren’t clearly seen, and to decide management, your doctor will likely correlate this MRI with pelvic ultrasound, blood tests (tumor markers), and your symptoms and exam.

Typical next steps
- Referral to a gynecologist or a gynecologic surgeon.
- Blood tests (tumor markers) as requested.
- Possible pelvic ultrasound for more detail.
- If it is a dermoid and depending on size, symptoms, and test results, options range from monitoring to surgical removal (often by laparoscopy). Surgery is commonly recommended for larger cysts or if there are symptoms or uncertainty.

When to seek urgent care
- New or severe lower abdominal pain, fever, vomiting, fainting, or signs of sudden worsening: this could indicate ovarian torsion or rupture and needs immediate attention.

If you want, tell me:
- Any current symptoms (pain, fullness, menstrual changes), and whether you have had an ultrasound or blood tests yet. I can help you prepare questions for your doctor.
